name: Retail
blurb: Demand forecasting, recommendation, and customer-service automation at volume, with NRF, Coresight, and IHL tracking the deployments.

points.desc: The Census BTOS series reports AI use for retail trade alongside every other sector, updated fortnightly.
points.name: Adoption is measured, not guessed

points.desc: The National Retail Federation covers store automation, inventory computer vision, and customer-experience software - the trade body's research is where retail AI adoption gets counted.
points.name: NRF tracks store technology

points.desc: Retail research firm producing adoption rates and market sizing for AI in merchandising and supply-chain logistics.
points.name: Coresight sizes the market

points.name: IHL measures the software spend

summary: Demand forecasting, recommendation, and customer-service automation are the volume use cases.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Business Outlook Survey recorded 15.5% of retail trade firms answering yes when asked whether they had used AI in the prior two weeks, a figure that held flat across the two most recent reporting periods. That places retail in the middle tier of measured adoption across all sectors the Census Bureau tracks, suggesting meaningful but far from universal deployment among the roughly half-million firms the NAICS 44-45 classification covers.

The National Retail Federation, the trade body whose research is where retail AI adoption gets counted, frames the current moment as a transition point, describing at its NRF Nexus 2026 conference the challenge of moving AI initiatives beyond experimentation and into deployments that generate culture, influence, and trust at scale. That framing implies that while pilots are widespread, production-grade rollouts remain unevenly distributed across the sector.

On the operational side, IHL Group, which tracks retail technology expenditure and return across grocery, apparel, and general merchandise, reports that inventory distortion has fallen to 1.7 trillion dollars but that empty shelves still represent a 690.9 billion dollar cost, with AI agents increasingly positioned to close that remaining gap. IHL also highlights specific vendor deployments: Boot Barn's fiscal Q1 2027 ecommerce sales grew 13.4%, with Salesforce's intent-aware discovery and agentic AI tools credited with boosting search relevance and preserving brand voice, while Crocs signed a ten-year agreement with Infosys to deploy AI-first solutions aimed at unifying data and enabling real-time decision-making across enterprise operations.

Coresight Research, which produces adoption rates and market sizing for AI in merchandising and supply-chain logistics, positions personalization, category management, and private label development as the use cases most actively being transformed by data science and AI, and convenes an invite-only forum specifically focused on the opportunities and challenges AI presents for consumer-facing businesses.

For a retailer evaluating deployment, the data collectively suggest that the clearest near-term return cases cluster around inventory management, search and discovery, and supply-chain logistics, where IHL's cost figures give quantified stakes. Vendor concentration is visible in the deals IHL surfaces, with Salesforce and Infosys among the named partners, though the sources do not report market share figures. The NRF's framing of experimentation as the current norm is a practical caution: the 15.5% Census figure counts any AI use in a two-week window, so measured adoption overstates the depth of integration at many firms, and a deploying retailer should expect organizational and data-readiness barriers to be as consequential as the technology selection itself.
